A password or PIN is considered personal information, your finger is not.

According to the 4th and 5th Amendments, you can not be required to self incriminate through intellectual property.

Your fingerprint is physical property, and can therefore be used against your will. Your password is intellectual property, and you are, in no way, obligated to share that with police or the court system. If you write your password down on a piece of paper, that paper, and its contents, are now physical property... and can be leveraged as such, with a warrant.
Doesn't mean it shouldn't be seen, debated, and talked about.

The entire affair has raised a number of legal questions, mostly centered on whether pressing one's finger on a device could be considered self-incriminating.

While the public may (should?) still ask and debate these questions, there are no "legal questions" here. The author failed to cite the precedents supporting this warrant or failed to do the most basic research. Either way, it is bad journalism.
